quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Search surname 'Voss' in Rowan County, NC; also try variants 'Boss' and 'Foss' (V/B and V/F confusion common in records transcribed from German script). A male Voss head with children of ages consistent with a mid-1830s marriage is the target — his given name and birth year will scope the probate search (items 3–4). Note: the 1850 US Federal Census was not returned by this session's collections_search, but a search of FamilySearch for Rowan County, NC in 1850 should also be attempted — Caroline would be approximately 11 and almost certainly in her father's household, making it the highest-yield census year.

If the 1860 search does not identify the father, he may still have been alive in 1870 (Caroline's father, born perhaps 1800-1820, would be 50-70 years old in 1870). collections_search returned the United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024), name-searchable (personCount above 0). The research question asks specifically which probate or estate record names Caroline Voss's father. A will, administration bond, inventory, or final settlement for a male Voss in Rowan County would name his children as heirs — naming Caroline as a daughter is direct parentage evidence. collections_search returned 'North Carolina, Rowan County Probate Records, 1753-1970' (collection 4000201), name-searchable (personCount above 0). Full-text keyword co-occurrence search of image group 004900301 ('Rowan County, North Carolina Probate Records, 1839-1899'), which loc_001 confirms is full-text searchable. The locality guide flags that only approximately 40% of the probate index is name-indexed, making full-text search more reliable than a name browse alone for this collection. Search requires both 'Voss' and 'Caroline' to appear in the same document, catching estate files where Caroline is named as an heir even when the father's name is not surfaced by the partial index. Fallback for item 3: this method reaches records item 3's name search will miss; it is not a duplicate but a complementary retrieval strategy.

The surname 'Voss' is of German origin, pointing to a Lutheran or Reformed congregation — both well established in Rowan County by the 1830s. A baptism entry for Caroline (born 1839) would directly name her father as the primary informant, making this a primary-source, primary-information record for the question. North Carolina did not have civil birth registration in 1839 (loc_001 notes civil death registration did not begin until 1913; civil birth registration was similarly late), so church registers are the earliest systematic source. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. entry.rationale: The Württemberg Familienregister (parish family register) was maintained by Protestant parishes from approximately 1808 and records complete family units — parents and all children listed under them. This is the single most efficient record type for Württemberg parentage research: a Seeger entry would directly name Katharina's father and mother (including the mother's maiden name), list all siblings, and state the family's residence. The Evangelische Kirche Baiersbronn register is browse-only (personCount 0) on Archion at https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn

Katharina's own baptism entry (born c. 1843) would name her father and mother directly — the most direct parentage evidence. The Taufregister (baptism register) of Evangelische Kirche Baiersbronn is browse-only (personCount 0) on Archion at the Baiersbronn parish page. Browse within approximately 1840-1847 given the birth estimate. Consider variant spellings such as Seger and Säger when reading entries.

Required for any parentage plan: the parents' Heiratsregister entry confirms them as a couple and supplies the mother's maiden name, which census and burial records typically omit. The Heiratsregister of Evangelische Kirche Baiersbronn is browse-only (personCount 0) on Archion. Its date before Katharina's c. 1843 birth corroborates paternity otherwise supported only by indirect evidence. Note: the marriage record alone does not prove Katharina is their child — her Taufregister entry or the Familienregister must place her with them. If no Seeger marriage is found in Baiersbronn, the parents may have married in a neighboring parish before settling there.

FAN item — required for a parentage question. Searching the Taufregister for other Seeger children baptized in Baiersbronn in the years surrounding Katharina's birth c. 1843 would name the same parents in each entry, corroborating parentage even if Katharina's own entry is difficult to read. Each sibling's baptism names the father and mother. The register is browse-only (personCount 0) on Archion at the Baiersbronn parish page. The same browse session used for pli_002 will cover most of this range; note every Seeger baptism entry found across 1830-1860.

If Katharina died in or near Baiersbronn, a burial or death entry would state her age and parentage. Pre-1870 entries are in the parish Sterberegister, browse-only on Archion at the Baiersbronn parish page. From 1 January 1870, Württemberg civil registration (Standesamt) took over; those records may also appear on Archion or at the Landesarchiv Baden-Württemberg. Katharina, born c. 1843, could plausibly have died anywhere from the 1860s to approximately 1920 — the lifespan window sets this item's bounds. This is a fallback if the Familienregister (pli_001) does not directly answer the question.

If Katharina or her family emigrated from Württemberg, emigration applications and lists compiled by Württemberg authorities named the emigrant's place of origin, age, family members, and sometimes parents. These records are held at the Landesarchiv Baden-Württemberg. A family emigration entry could confirm Katharina's parentage or identify her parents' names where the local parish registers do not. This is a fallback if the Archion parish-register searches (pli_001 through pli_004) and the death records (pli_005) do not resolve the question.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) has no recorded death date in the project tree. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already cataloged in the tree but has never been searched — zero assertions reference it. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 collection on FamilySearch is browse-only (personCount 0); this requires an image browse of Schuylkill County probate dockets, not a name search. A will naming Patrick as a son is the strongest direct parentage evidence available and would move the conclusion from Probable to Proved. If Thomas died intestate, the administration bond or inventory may list heirs including Patrick, which is still direct evidence. Thomas born ~1818 could plausibly have died from the 1850s through the 1900s; the date range covers his full realistic lifespan from Patrick's birth. This is the primary remaining gap identified in the proof summary.

The 1880 U.S. census introduced the relationship-to-head column, absent in 1850 and 1860. If Patrick (age ~35 in 1880) still appears in Thomas's (age ~62) household and the schedule records 'son,' that is direct evidence of parentage from a contemporaneous record — stronger than either prior census. Even if Patrick heads his own household by 1880, the schedule names his neighbors, who form the FAN cluster that may independently document the family. Thomas's own 1880 household (if found) names any other children still at home, identifying siblings whose records corroborate the family structure. The 1880 census is listed as a remaining gap in the proof summary.

The 1870 census bridges the gap between the 1860 entry (Patrick age 15 in Thomas's household) and the 1880 household, showing whether Patrick remained in Thomas's home into adulthood or established his own household. Thomas would be ~52 and Patrick ~25 in 1870. Though the 1870 census still lacks the relationship column, finding both men in the same township — or showing Patrick living adjacent to Thomas — strengthens the FAN-cluster pattern and confirms geographic continuity. Neighbors recorded in the same dwelling series form a cluster to cross-reference with church and land records. The 1870 census is listed as a remaining gap in the proof summary.

The 1900 census records parents' birthplaces for every enumerated person. Patrick (age ~55 in 1900) almost certainly heads his own household by this date. His entry will show his wife, children, and parents' birthplaces — if both parents are listed as Ireland-born, that is consistent with Thomas Flynn of Ireland and gives a cross-check against the census co-residence pattern. Neighbors in Patrick's 1900 schedule may overlap with families whose records name Thomas Flynn, extending the FAN cluster. The 1900 census is listed as a remaining gap in the proof summary.

A dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage record is required for every parentage plan. The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable (personCount 982415). Thomas born ~1818 would plausibly have married between 1838 and 1852 (before or around Patrick's birth ~1845); the date range extends to 1855 to account for a later or second marriage. The marriage record (a) identifies Patrick's mother's maiden name, which census and death records consistently omit, (b) confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple before Patrick's birth, and (c) by its date relative to ~1845, corroborates that Thomas is a plausible father — though the marriage record alone does not place Patrick with the parents and so cannot by itself establish the parentage link. Variant spellings (Flinn, Flin, Flinn) should be used in the search.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record, searched in the Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records collection (name-searchable, personCount 982415). Roman Catholic church marriage registers in the anthracite coal region routinely name the groom's father. A record stating 'Patrick Flynn, son of Thomas Flynn' would be direct evidence of parentage that is independent of the census co-residence pattern and the secondary death certificate informant (James Brown). Patrick born ~1845 would typically marry in his early-to-mid twenties; the range 1862–1885 covers a generous window. Variant surname spellings should be used.

A search for baptism and burial records of other children of Thomas Flynn — siblings of Patrick — in the Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable, personCount 982415). The 1850 census household included Thomas and Patrick; the household may include additional children not yet individually identified in the project. A sibling's baptism record naming 'Thomas Flynn' and his wife as parents, combined with Patrick's appearance in the same household, builds a corroborating pattern of Thomas's acknowledged children and establishes the family unit independently of census co-residence. Date range covers siblings born roughly 1843–1865, assuming Thomas and his wife were fertile from around Patrick's birth through Thomas's likely middle age. This is a FAN item: a sibling's record names the subject's parent directly.

Deed records for Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County. Boundary recitals in deeds name adjoining landowners — those neighbors form the core FAN cluster around Thomas and are the same families to cross-reference with church and probate records. A deed conveying land from Thomas to Patrick would be direct evidence of the father-son relationship; a deed naming Patrick as a witness or co-grantor identifies him as an associate of Thomas. Deeds recorded after Thomas's death and signed by his heirs may name Patrick collectively with siblings as grantors, identifying the full sibling set. Thomas born ~1818 in an anthracite coal community may have held mining leases or surface lots; the date range covers his working life through the period when heirs would have settled the estate. A specific FamilySearch collection id was not returned by collections_search for Schuylkill County land records; search via the FamilySearch catalog for Schuylkill County deed books, or check the county courthouse as a fallback.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
